front: Name the five organelles the lesson lists for a typical animal cell.
answer: Nucleus / Cytoplasm / Cell membrane / Mitochondria / Ribosomes
title: Cell Structure and Microscopy

front: Name the three extra structures the lesson gives that plant cells have, beyond animal cell organelles.
answer: Chloroplasts / Permanent vacuole / Cell wall
title: Cell Structure and Microscopy

front: Why is a coverslip lowered onto a microscope slide at an angle?
answer: Lowering the coverslip at an angle avoids trapping air bubbles, which would distort the image.
title: Cell Structure and Microscopy

front: Why is a red blood cell shaped like a biconcave disc?
answer: Its biconcave disc shape increases the surface area available for absorbing oxygen.
title: Cell Structure and Microscopy

front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that affect the rate of diffusion.
answer: Concentration gradient / Temperature / Surface area / Distance travelled
title: Cell Division and Transport

front: How does mitosis produce two genetically identical daughter cells?
answer: One full set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell before the cytoplasm and cell membrane divide in two.
title: Cell Division and Transport

front: Why do root hair cells need active transport, not diffusion, to absorb mineral ions from the soil?
answer: Mineral ions are at a lower concentration in the soil than in the root hair cell, so moving them in needs energy to go against the gradient.
title: Cell Division and Transport

front: Name the five levels of organisation the lesson gives, from cells to organism.
answer: Cells / Tissues / Organs / Organ systems / Organism
title: Organisation and the Digestive System

front: Name the four food substances the lesson gives food tests for.
answer: Starch / Sugars / Proteins / Lipids
title: Organisation and the Digestive System

front: Why does bile emulsify fats in the small intestine?
answer: Bile breaks fats into smaller droplets, which increases the surface area for lipase to work on.
title: Organisation and the Digestive System

front: Why is enzyme action described using the lock-and-key model?
answer: Only a substrate with a shape matching the enzyme's active site can fit, like a key fitting one specific lock.
title: Organisation and the Digestive System

front: Name the three types of blood vessel the lesson gives.
answer: Arteries / Veins / Capillaries
title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

front: Name the four components of blood the lesson gives.
answer: Red blood cells / White blood cells / Platelets / Plasma
title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

front: Why can coronary heart disease lead to a heart attack?
answer: Fatty deposits narrow the coronary arteries, and if the heart muscle doesn't get enough oxygen it can trigger a heart attack.
title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

front: Why are heart transplants a limited treatment option for coronary heart disease?
answer: Heart transplants are limited by the availability of donors and the risk that the patient's immune system rejects the new heart.
title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

front: Name the four key risk factors for non-communicable disease the lesson gives.
answer: Smoking / Obesity / Alcohol / Lack of exercise
title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues

front: Name the five main plant tissues the lesson gives.
answer: Epidermal tissue / Palisade mesophyll / Spongy mesophyll / Xylem / Phloem
title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues

front: How does evaporation of water from leaves cause water to move up through the xylem?
answer: Water evaporates and diffuses out through the stomata, and this creates a continuous transpiration stream that pulls water up through the xylem.
title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues

front: Why doesn't a risk factor being linked to a disease prove that it causes the disease?
answer: A risk factor is correlated with the disease and makes it more likely, but correlation does not always prove causation.
title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues

front: Name the four main types of pathogen the lesson gives.
answer: Bacteria / Viruses / Fungi / Protists
title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences

front: Name the four ways the lesson gives that pathogens can be transmitted between organisms.
answer: Air / Water / Direct contact / Vectors
title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences

front: Why do viruses often destroy the host cell they infect?
answer: Viruses take over the cell's machinery to make copies of themselves, which often destroys the cell in the process.
title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences

front: Why does the secondary immune response usually prevent illness, unlike the primary response?
answer: Memory cells let the body produce antibodies much faster and more strongly on second exposure than during the slower first response.
title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences

front: Name the three stages of drug development the lesson gives.
answer: Preclinical testing / Clinical trials / Peer review and approval
title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development

front: Name the three ways the lesson gives to reduce the development of antibiotic resistance.
answer: Only prescribe when necessary / Patients complete the full course / Restrict agricultural use
title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development

front: Why do painkillers not cure an infection?
answer: Painkillers treat symptoms of disease, such as pain, but do not kill the pathogens causing the infection.
title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development

front: Why is a new drug tested on cells, tissues and live animals before human trials?
answer: This preclinical testing checks whether the drug is toxic, whether it works, and what dose is needed.
title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development

front: Name the three limiting factors of photosynthesis the lesson gives.
answer: Light intensity / Carbon dioxide concentration / Temperature
title: Photosynthesis and Respiration

front: Name the five uses of glucose in plants the lesson gives.
answer: Respiration / Converted to starch for storage / Producing cellulose for cell walls / Producing amino acids for proteins / Producing lipids for storage
title: Photosynthesis and Respiration

front: How does light intensity change as distance from a light source increases?
answer: Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source, so it falls off rapidly with distance.
title: Photosynthesis and Respiration

front: Why do muscles produce lactic acid during intense exercise?
answer: During intense exercise the muscles can't get enough oxygen for aerobic respiration, so anaerobic respiration happens too and produces lactic acid.
title: Photosynthesis and Respiration

front: Name the five ways the lesson gives to identify plant disease.
answer: Stunted growth / Spots on leaves / Areas of decay or rot / Discolouration / Malformed stems or leaves
title: Culturing Microorganisms and Plant Disease

front: Name the three types of plant defence the lesson gives.
answer: Physical barriers / Chemical defences / Mechanical adaptations
title: Culturing Microorganisms and Plant Disease

front: Why does rose black spot reduce a plant's ability to photosynthesise?
answer: Infected leaves turn yellow and drop early, reducing the area of leaf available for photosynthesis.
title: Culturing Microorganisms and Plant Disease

front: How does the bacterium that causes crown gall disease produce tumour-like growths?
answer: Agrobacterium tumefaciens inserts its DNA into plant cells, which causes tumour-like growths on stems and roots.
title: Culturing Microorganisms and Plant Disease

front: Name the five steps the lesson gives for producing monoclonal antibodies, in order.
items: Fused with tumour cells into hybridomas
Hybridoma cells screened for right antibody
answer: Mouse injected with target antigen / Lymphocytes collected from the spleen / Fused with tumour cells into hybridomas / Hybridoma cells screened for right antibody / Selected cells cloned and grown
title: Monoclonal Antibodies

front: Name the three limitations of monoclonal antibodies the lesson gives.
items: Don't yet give hoped-for miracle cures
answer: Can cause unexpected side effects / Expensive to develop and produce / Don't yet give hoped-for miracle cures
title: Monoclonal Antibodies

front: How do fluorescent dyes help researchers use monoclonal antibodies in laboratory research?
answer: Monoclonal antibodies tagged with fluorescent dyes let researchers see exactly where a particular protein is located within a cell.
title: Monoclonal Antibodies

front: Why are hybridoma cells screened after they are created?
answer: Hybridoma cells are screened to select only the ones that produce the correct, desired antibody.
title: Monoclonal Antibodies
